1:
What Moses brought down from the cloud, and what he left behind, is the first thing Henry settles. We may suppose, he says, that when Moses went into the midst of the cloud and abode there so long, where the holy angels attended the divine Majesty, he saw and heard very glorious things relating to the upper world; but they were things which it was not lawful nor possible to utter, and therefore in the records he kept of the transactions there he says nothing to satisfy the curiosity of those who would intrude into the things they have not seen, but writes only that which he was to speak to the children of Israel — for Scripture is designed to direct us in our duty, not to fill our heads with speculations nor to please our fancies. Wesley repeats the judgement almost word for word. Gill fixes the two moments the verses hold apart, that the Lord spake to Moses when on the mount and in the midst of the cloud, and that the speaking to Israel was to come when he should go down from the mountain to the camp.

Why a sanctuary at all is answered most fully by Keil and Delitzsch. It was to give a definite external form to the covenant concluded with his people, and to construct a visible bond of fellowship in which he might manifest himself to them and they might draw near to him as their God; and its construction and arrangement were determined in all respects by God himself, who showed Moses a pattern upon the mountain and prescribed with great minuteness both the form and the materials of every part. If the sanctuary was to answer its purpose, they argue, the erection of it could not be left to the inventive faculty of any man whatever, but must proceed from him who was there to manifest himself as the Holy One in righteousness and grace, so that the people could only carry out what God appointed. Henry reaches the same place by another road, that God had chosen this people to be a peculiar people to himself and would be their King, and that having already given them laws he now orders a royal palace to be set up among them, a palace which is at once ceremonial and typical.
2:
The manner of the giving is where the witnesses linger. Ellicott observes that God, being about to command the construction of a dwelling for himself such as the circumstances of the case allowed, prefaced his directions about materials and form by inviting the people to contribute from their stores; the erection of sanctuaries, he adds, is one of the fittest occasions for man to show his gratitude to God by giving to him of his own, largely and liberally. On the qualifying clause he gives the Hebrew as of every man whose heart impels him, and states the rule bluntly, that unless gifts come from the heart they are an offence to God, who loves a cheerful giver. Henry insists it was not by a tax imposed upon them but by a voluntary contribution, and Wesley that it was not prescribed what or how much they must give but left to their generosity, that they might show their good will to the house of God. Clarke explains the term itself, a kind of free-will offering consisting of anything necessary for the occasion, properly meaning anything lifted up, since in presenting it to God it was lifted up to be laid on his altar; and he supplies the political sense of the whole arrangement, that God required a tent suited in some sort to his dignity because he was to act as their king, and that bringing presents was held to be the duty of every subject appearing before his prince.

Calvin spends his longest note here not on the offering but on the date, answering an opinion that the tabernacle was built and set up before Moses brought down the first tables. Three reasons were urged for it: that a tabernacle is mentioned immediately after Moses came down with the tables and broke them; that Moses is told to put into the ark a testimony he had not yet received, so that he must have received it before the ark was made; and that when he exhorts the people to build he makes no mention of their apostasy and idolatry, which suggests they had not yet fallen. Calvin answers each in turn. The tent mentioned there was not the great tabernacle afterwards made for God's service, since that stood in the midst of the host and this was set without it, but Moses' own tent, whither the people had access to consult with God. What was described first was not the ark but the form the ark should take, which was shown in the Mount and executed afterwards. And the silence about the fault is not evidence of innocence, since the people had already received correction and Moses had removed his tent in sign of God's indignation, while those touched with remorse showed themselves the more cheerful in God's service as a sign of true repentance, and Moses would not be still harping upon the same string lest he discourage them altogether.

His own reasons for the later date are three as well, and they are arithmetical rather than exegetical. Moses is bidden to make the tabernacle according to all that the Lord should show him in the Mount, and the form was first shown him during the forty days and nights at the end of which he received the tables, so the tabernacle could not have been made before its fashion was shown. The tabernacle was reared up in the first month of the second year, and the camp removed from Sinai about a month and a half later, which leaves no room for the two further absences of forty days each that the earlier dating would require. And by that dating a great part of the book must be transposed, everything concerning the making and setting up of the tabernacle being moved in front of the chapters that record the fall.
3:
The list is a list of alternatives, not a schedule of dues, and Gill says so first. Some one or other of the following things was to be taken of each of them that had a heart and had it in the power of his hands to give; it was not expected that something of each of these should be had of everyone, but every man was to give, and it was to be received of him, whatever of these would suit him best to bestow, as he was possessed of it and had a heart to give. Many of them, he adds, were abundantly supplied for the service from what they had brought out of Egypt, and since it was the Lord who gave them favour in the eyes of the Egyptians to lend or give them the riches they had, they were under the greater obligation to part with somewhat of it freely.

Calvin draws the moral of the variety rather than of the quantity. What the poor offer of their little will not be eclipsed by the abundance of the rich, since God deigns to reckon goats' hair among the sacred offerings not less than gold, purple and precious stones; and by the varied and manifold contributions he would show, as in a glass, that a variety of gifts are necessary to the building of the spiritual temple. The liberality of the rich was indeed more splendid, but as they did not scruple to mix their gold and silver, blue, purple and precious stones with brass, iron and other common materials, so also, now-a-days, those who aid the edification of the Church by their more excellent gifts admit poor brethren into fellowship without contempt or dislike, though it is not given to those brethren to equal them.

The three metals are then taken separately. Clarke distinguishes four Hebrew words for gold and assigns each a stage: one for gold shut up in the mine or in its ore, one for gold made current by being coined and stamped with the mark expressive of its value, one for wrought gold, pure and highly polished and probably used for overlaying or gilding, and one denoting solidity and compactness and probably meaning gold formed into plate. The third of these is the word here, he says, because it was in a state capable of being variously manufactured for the service of the sanctuary. Silver he derives from a root meaning pale or wan or white, from its well-known colour; and brass he takes for copper, unless the factitious metal be meant, which is formed by combining the ore of zinc with copper, and he notes that because it took so fine a polish and kept its lustre it was used among ancient nations for weapons of war and defensive armour. Ellicott asks instead whether they could afford it, and answers that they could: they had brought out of Egypt both their ancestral wealth and the rich gifts received at the moment of their departure, and had added to it by the plunder of the Amalekites, so that there is no difficulty in supposing they furnished the gold without seriously impoverishing themselves. The silver, comparatively small in amount, appears ultimately to have been furnished in another way, and the brass, or rather bronze, since brass seems to have been unknown at this time, was small in amount and of no great value.
4:
What was being asked for is not a colour but a cloth, and Gill is careful about it. The Jewish doctors are much divided about the sense of these words, some taking one colour and some another; but by them we are to understand neither the colours themselves, which could not be brought, nor even the materials for dyeing them, but wool or cloths, silken or linen, of those colours, made up into yarn and woven, which were much used in the garments of the priests, in the curtains of the tabernacle and in the vail between the holy and the most holy place. Ellicott agrees on the point, that linen yarn of the three colours seems to have been what the people were asked to furnish. Wesley disposes of the whole clause in five words, that they were materials of those colours.

On what the three colours actually were, Clarke and Ellicott work from different evidence and arrive close together. Clarke takes the first for an azure or sky colour, rendered by the old versions a sky-blue or deep violet; the second for a very precious colour extracted from a shell-fish, supposed to be the famous Tyrian purple, so costly and so much celebrated in antiquity; and the third from a word signifying a worm, of which the colouring matter was made, joined to another signifying to repeat or double, which implies that to strike this colour the wool or cloth was twice dipped — whence the old rendering of scarlet twice dyed, and whence too, through the name the Arabs give it, the French and English words for crimson. Ellicott names the sources: a dark blue produced from indigo, which was the only blue known to the Egyptians; a purplish crimson derived from the murex, the main source of the Tyrian dye of the ancients; and a scarlet furnished by the cochineal insect of the holm oak, largely employed in antiquity though now superseded by the brighter tint obtained from the insect of Mexico.

The fine linen and the goats' hair divide the same way, a philological answer against an observed one. Clarke reports that whether the word means linen, cotton or silk is not agreed among interpreters, and that because the term also signifies six the rabbins suppose it always means the fine linen of Egypt, in which six folds constituted one thread. Ellicott answers from the mummy cloths, that it is white thread spun from flax, found to be the material of almost all the Egyptian dresses and other undyed fabrics, of a yellowish white, soft and wonderfully fine and delicate. On the goats' hair Clarke observes that in parts of Asia Minor, Syria, Cilicia and Phrygia the goats have long, fine and beautiful hair, in some cases almost as fine as silk, which is sheared at proper times and manufactured into garments, and he quotes the poet who reckoned it nearly of equal value with wool, the shepherd easing the loaded herds of their hoary beards to make cloth warm in tents for the soldier and a shield for the shivering mariner. Ellicott points at the present rather than the past: the covering of an Arab tent is to this day almost always of goats' hair, an excellent fabric being woven from the soft inner hair of the Syrian goat and a coarse one from the outer coat, and the yarn was asked for so that from it might be produced the first of the three outer coverings of the tabernacle.
5:
The red rams draw two quite different kinds of evidence. Clarke reads the phrase literally as the skins of red rams and defends that sense from natural history: many respectable travellers attest that in the Levant sheep are often met with that have red or violet-coloured fleeces, and almost all ancient writers speak of the same thing, one describing the rams of Polyphemus as having a violet-coloured fleece; from facts of this kind, he suggests, the fable of the golden fleece very probably had its origin. He adds what he has seen himself, sheep in the Zetland Isles with fleeces white, black, and chocolate. Ellicott looks to the tanneries instead: North Africa has always been celebrated for the production of the best possible leather, brilliant colours always were and still are affected by the North African races, and their red skins have been famous in all ages, so that the Israelites had probably brought many skins of this kind out of Egypt.

The second kind of skin is the hardest word in the chapter, and the witnesses divide over whether it names an animal at all. Clarke reports that few terms have afforded greater perplexity to commentators, and follows the scholar who seems to him to have proved that no animal is intended but a colour: none of the ancient versions acknowledges an animal except the Chaldee, which seems to think the badger, and from it our own translation is borrowed, while the older Greek and Latin have skins dyed violet, the Syriac azure, the Arabic black, the Coptic violet and the modern Persic simply ram-skins. Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch both keep the animal and move it into the sea. Ellicott objects that the badger is not a native of North Africa nor of the Arabian desert, so that the rendering is a very improbable conjecture, and notes that the Arabic word is the name of a marine animal resembling the seal, or is applied with some vagueness to seals, dugongs, dolphins, sharks and dog-fish. Keil and Delitzsch settle on the sea-cow of the Red Sea, and observe that in it the upper skin is larger, thicker and coarser than the under, which is only two lines thick and very tough, so that the one would serve for the thick covering of tents and the other for ornamental sandals.

On the wood there is no such division, only a question of species. Clarke reports it supposed by some to be the finest kind of cedar and by others the acacia, a species of thorn, solid, light and very beautiful, and argues from supply: it was plentiful in Egypt and abounds in Arabia Deserta, the very place in which Moses was when he built the tabernacle, so it is reasonable to suppose he built it of that wood. Ellicott treats the identification as settled and reasons the same way, that it was certainly not the palm and that there are no trees in that region from which boards could be cut except the palm and the acacia; he describes it as a gnarled and thorny tree, somewhat like a solitary hawthorn in habit but much larger, concedes that at present it does not grow there to a size admitting of planks ten cubits long, and answers that it attains such a size further north and may formerly have done so here. The wood itself he calls hard and close-grained, of an orange colour with a darker heart, well adapted for cabinet work. Calvin quotes the naturalists to the same effect and adds the observation that the most important material, the wood for the tent, is just the one found there most plentifully, and that the Greek translators thought it good enough to name it wood that never decays. Wesley says only that it grew in Egypt and the deserts of Arabia and was very durable and precious.
6:
The two clauses about oil and spices are read as assumptions carried forward, and Ellicott sets them out as such. It is assumed that the sanctuary to be built will need lighting, and oil is therefore provided for it; assumed again that anointing oil will be needed and spices a necessary ingredient in it, since the tabernacle, all its vessels and the priests appointed to serve in it had afterwards to be consecrated by anointing; and assumed in the third clause that there would be incense to burn. Gill identifies the oil as olive oil on the authority of the old Jewish versions. Clarke raises the practical objection and half answers it: the oil they must have brought with them from Egypt, for they could not get any in the wilderness where there were no olives, though it is likely that this and some other directions refer more to what was to be done when they were in their fixed and settled residence than while they were still wandering. The spices, he adds, abounded in different parts of these countries. Keil and Delitzsch note that the word rendered sweet incense means literally the scents, because the materials of which it was composed were not all of them fragrant.

The stones are the one item on which every witness confesses that he does not know. Gill says they are so called from their likeness to the nail of a man's finger, and lists the renderings against each other: beryl in the old versions, sardius in the Greek, and sardonyx in the judgement of those who think the stone had a likeness both to the onyx and to the sardius. Ellicott counts the same disagreement and concludes plainly that there is considerable doubt what stone is meant; he adds the useful arithmetic that only three such stones seem to have been required, one for the breastplate and two for the shoulder-pieces. Keil and Delitzsch prefer beryls, gloss the second phrase literally as stones of filling, that is jewels that are set, and record that the precious stones were presented by the princes of the congregation. Clarke admits the difficulty as frankly and then offers a guess from his own cabinet, that it might have been the fine pale stone called the Egyptian pebble, specimens of which lay before him as he wrote, brought from the coast of the Red Sea by a friend for his collection of minerals.

What the stones were to be set in gets a long description from Clarke, who admits at the outset that it is very difficult to tell what the ephod was or in what form it was made. It was a garment peculiar to the priests and essential to all the parts of divine worship, since without it no person attempted to inquire of God; and because the root of the word means to tie or bind close, he follows the conjecture that it was a kind of girdle brought from behind the neck and over the shoulders, hanging down before, crossed upon the stomach and carried round the waist. Where it crossed on the breast there was a square ornament, the breastplate, in which twelve precious stones were set, each bearing one of the names of the twelve sons of Jacob. There were two sorts, one of plain linen for the priests and one much embroidered for the high priest, the latter of gold, blue, purple, scarlet and fine twisted linen, fastened on the shoulders with two precious stones engraved with the names of the twelve tribes, six on each — stones different from those of the breastplate, with which they have been confounded. He ends by preferring a second guess, that it was a garment like that worn by heralds, covering back, breast and belly, open at the sides and probably without sleeves.
8:
The whole list of gifts has been running toward this sentence, and Ellicott says so plainly: the enumeration of the offerings has been subordinate to it. Hitherto Israel had had no place of worship, no structure dedicated to God, and God now brings that state of things to an end. In Egypt they had seen structures of vast size and extraordinary magnificence erected in every city for the worship of the Egyptian gods; they are now to have their own structure, their holy place, their house of God. Gill defines the word simply, a holy place to dwell in, so called from his dwelling in it; Clarke narrows it to that part of the tabernacle which was called the most holy place, into which the high priest entered only once a year on the great day of atonement.

Why the house had to be a tent is Ellicott's next point, and it is a practical one. They were still in a nomadic condition, without fixed abode and continually shifting their quarters, so that a building in the ordinary sense of the word would have been unsuitable; they must soon have quitted it, or have foregone their hopes of Palestine. God therefore devised for them a structure in harmony with their condition, a tent-temple modelled on the ordinary form of the better Oriental tents but made of the best materials and of an unusual size, and still portable. Keil and Delitzsch put the same thing as a transaction: with these freewill-offerings they were to make the Lord a sanctuary, that he might dwell in the midst of them.

The promise attached to it is what Calvin thinks moves the giving. By first setting before them an inestimable recompense, he says, God stirs up the people to give largely; for although liberality is praised by all as a most excellent virtue, no one willingly deprives himself of his own to bestow it upon others, since all think it so much lost to themselves unless they have some compensation in view. Wherefore, that they may expend cheerfully, God promises that he will dwell among them, than which nothing is more desirable.

What such dwelling can mean is then guarded on every side. Calvin warns that we must beware of imagining anything inconsistent with the nature of God, for he who sits above the heavens and whose footstool is the earth could not be enclosed in the tabernacle; but because in his indulgence for the infirmities of an ignorant people he desired to testify the presence of his grace and help by a visible symbol, the earthly sanctuary is called his dwelling amongst men, inasmuch as there he was not worshipped in vain. It was not the infinite essence of God that dwelt there, he insists, but his name, or the record of his name. Wesley compresses the whole caution into a clause, that it is not by his essence, which is everywhere, but by his grace and glorious operations. Ellicott comes at it from the other end and will not let the concession empty the promise: though God dwelleth not in temples made with hands, is not confined to them and cannot be comprehended within them, yet since it pleases him to manifest himself especially in such abodes he may well be said to dwell there in a peculiar manner; and his dwelling with Israel was not purely spiritual, since from time to time he manifested himself sensibly in the Holy of Holies, where he dwelt continually and might be consulted by the temporal ruler of the nation.
9:
The clause about the pattern is read by Gill as an instruction about workmanship: the sanctuary was to be made in all respects exactly according to the view of it that Moses now had upon the mount from God, and which he was to communicate to the workmen for their instruction and direction. Calvin hears a prohibition in it as much as a direction, that the artificers should copy the pattern shown to Moses and not dare to invent anything, since it would be a profanation to mix up anything human with the commands of God. Clarke reports an older opinion that there had been a tabernacle before the one Moses erected, though it probably did not then exist, and that the new one was to be formed exactly on the model of that ancient one; and he glosses the word itself as meaning literally the dwelling or habitation, so called because it was the dwelling place of God and the only place on earth in which he made himself manifest.

What kind of thing the pattern was is a question Ellicott states as a choice of three. It has been maintained that God showed Moses a material structure furnished with material objects, as the model he was to follow; or a pictorial representation of the whole; or a series of visions in which the forms were represented to the eye of the mind. The entire analogy of the divine dealings, he judges, is in favour of the last. Keil and Delitzsch argue a narrower question of tense in the same sentence, against those who take the showing as already finished: the participle does not refer to the past, and nothing indicates that it does; nor does it follow from the later expression about what is showed thee in the mount that Moses had by then left the mountain and returned to the camp. The past tenses in the parallel passages, they suggest, may be explained either by supposing that the sight of the model of the whole building preceded the description of the several things required for it, or by taking the instructions to make each part in such and such a way as pointing back to that sight.

Wesley turns the minuteness of the instructions into an argument about Scripture itself. God showed him an exact plan of it in little, which he must conform to in all points, and did not only show him the model but gave him particular directions how to frame the tabernacle according to that model in all the parts of it. Then the comparison: when Moses was to describe the creation of the world, stately and curious a fabric as it is, he gave a very short and general account of it, but when he comes to describe the tabernacle he does it with the greatest niceness and accuracy imaginable — for God's church and instituted religion is more precious to him than all the rest of the world, and the Scriptures were written not to describe to us the works of nature, a general view of which is enough to lead us to the knowledge of the Creator, but to acquaint us with the methods of grace and those things which are purely matters of revelation.
10:
The first thing ordered is the chest, and Henry marks its place in the design: the ark with its appurtenances is the furniture of the most holy place and the special token of God's presence, for which the tabernacle was erected to be the receptacle. Ellicott insists on the word. The term rendered ark here is an entirely different word from the one so translated of the vessel that rode the flood and of the basket among the reeds; this one properly means a chest or coffer of small dimensions, used to contain money or other valuables, and in one place applied to a mummy-case. Clarke gives the same range — an ark, chest, coffer or coffin — and adds that it was the most excellent of all the holy things belonging to the Mosaic economy, that for its sake the tabernacle and the temple were built, and that it conferred a sanctity wherever it was fixed.

The dimensions are converted by several witnesses, and they agree within inches. Henry, reckoning the cubit at twenty-one inches on the computation that it was three inches longer than our half-yard, makes the chest about fifty-two inches long, thirty-one broad and thirty-one deep; Wesley repeats those figures exactly; Clarke, on the same cubit, gives about four feet five inches by two feet six by two feet six; Ellicott states it as three feet nine by two feet three by two feet three. Clarke then reasons backwards from the box to its contents: since the ark was chiefly intended to deposit the two tables of stone in, we may reasonably conjecture that the length of those tables was not less than four feet and their breadth not less than two; as to their thickness he will say nothing, since the depth of the ark was intended for other matters besides the tables, such as the rod and the pot of manna, though he thinks these were probably laid up beside the ark rather than in it.

Ellicott places the object in its setting: sacred coffers were important parts of the furniture of temples in Egypt, usually containing the image or emblem of some deity and constructed so as to be readily carried in processions. Gill reads the material for what it signifies, that the wood is an incorruptible wood which does not rot, rendered in the Greek by a word meaning exactly that, and takes it to denote the perpetuity of Christ in his person and in the natures united in it; and he runs through the names the ark is given elsewhere, the ark of God, the ark of his strength, the holy ark and the ark of the covenant, finding all suitable to one in whom the treasures of wisdom and knowledge lie as treasure lies in a coffer.

On the overlaying, Ellicott weighs a method against a method. It is possible but scarcely probable that gilding is intended: gilding was well known in Egypt long before the time of Moses and may have been within the artistic powers of some of the Hebrews, but it is a process requiring much apparatus, and less likely in the desert than the far simpler one of overlaying with gold plates, which would also have been thought more suitable because more valuable; and it is the Jewish tradition that gold plates were employed. Gill states the same conclusion in a line, that it was not gilded but had a plate of pure gold put over it. On the crown the witnesses differ only in vividness: Ellicott takes it for a rim or border carried round the edge of the chest at the top, and thinks its object was probably to keep the mercy-seat in place; Keil and Delitzsch call it a golden rim encircling the ark like an ornamental wreath; Clarke quotes the Greek, which has it as waves of gold wreathed round about.
12:
The rings are for carrying, and Ellicott explains both their number and their odd position. Though the ark was not to be carried in procession like the Egyptian arks, it would have to be carried when the Israelites resumed their journeyings, and the four rings were made to receive the two poles by which it was to be borne on the shoulders of the priests. The Hebrew, he notes, is literally at the four feet thereof: the rings were to be affixed not at the four upper corners of the chest but at the four bottom corners, so that the ark when carried on men's shoulders might be elevated above them and be in no danger of coming into contact with the bearers' persons. He grants the objection that such an arrangement might seem to endanger the equilibrium of the ark when carried, and answers with another scholar that the smallness of its dimensions rendered safe transportation, even with the rings at its feet, not impossible. Keil and Delitzsch describe the same fittings and translate the word for the feet as walking feet, feet bent as if for walking. Gill attends to the making rather than the placing — a mould was to be made, and the gold being melted was poured into it, and so the rings were fashioned — and says of the poles that they were of the same wood the ark was made of, covered with plates of gold so that they appeared to be all of gold, the wood not being seen.

That the poles were never to be withdrawn is given two reasons and raises one difficulty. Clarke reads it as readiness: the ark should ever be considered as in readiness to be removed, God not having told them at what hour he should command them to strike their tents. Ellicott reads it as danger: they were to remain always in the rings, whether the ark was in motion or at rest, so that there might never at any time be a necessity for touching the ark itself, or even the rings — and he who touched the ark imperilled his life. The difficulty is Clarke's own, and he states it against himself: if the poles were never to be taken out, how can another passage say that when the camp should set forward they should put in the staves thereof, which intimates that when they encamped they took them out? His reconciliation, offered with a great show of probability, is that besides the poles which passed through the rings there were two others in the form of a bier or handbarrow, on which the ark was laid to be transported once it and its own poles, still in their rings, had been wrapped in the covering of skins and blue cloth; the poles of the ark itself, which might be considered as handles simply to lift it by, were never taken out, but the bier was taken from under it when they encamped. Gill only insists on the word, that they were not only to be put into the rings but to remain in them, yea, always.
16:
What the testimony is draws the chapter's one properly theological dispute, and Calvin opens it. The title so often given to the law indicates that something more is contained in it than the rule of a just and holy life, namely the compact whereby God bound himself to his people and his people to himself — which is why the table of the covenant is afterwards used instead of the testimony, the word being equivalent to a contract, commonly called a convention. He carries the point through the Psalms, where the Prophet gives the name of testimonies not only to the Commandments but to whatever God delivered by the hand of Moses for the salvation of his people, and where the law and the testimony are named together not as two different things but so that the utility of the law may be commended, because it contains all that God would have testified to his people. Gill and Ellicott keep the narrower sense, Gill making it a testification of the mind and will of God, what he would have done or omitted, which would stand as a testimony against the Israelites should they transgress what they had declared their approbation of, and Ellicott calling it simply God's witness against sin. Clarke notes that the tables were not yet given, derives the word from a root meaning forward or onward, to bear witness to or of a person or thing, and widens the witness to everything the ark held, the rod and the pot of manna and the holy anointing oil bearing testimony to the Messiah in his prophetic, sacerdotal and regal offices along with the tables. Ellicott adds the consequence for the chest, that as containing them it was called the ark of the testimony.

Gill alone follows the deposit through to its application. That the law was laid up inside the ark and preserved there may signify, he says, that the law was in the heart of Christ, which he undertook to fulfil and with pleasure did; that he is become the fulfilling end of the law for righteousness to them that believe in him; and that it remains with him as a rule of walk and conversation to his people, so far as it is of a moral, holy and spiritual nature.
17:
What the covering should be called is the sharpest philological dispute in the chapter, and Ellicott names the parties. Those critics to whom the idea of expiation is unsatisfactory render the word by lid or cover; it may be admitted, he grants, that the simple verb has the physical meaning of covering, but the intensive form has never any other meaning than that of covering or expiating sins, and the noun is formed from the intensive. Hence the old Greek and Latin renderings, and the mercy seat of our version, are correct. Keil and Delitzsch argue the same case: the meaning lid cannot be sustained, notwithstanding that the thing was placed upon the ark and covered the tables within it, for the verb has not the literal signification of covering in either conjugation — in the one it occurs only where it means to pitch or tar, and in the other only in the figurative sense of covering up sin. Both call decisive the passage naming the holy of holies the house of expiation, which cannot possibly mean the covering-house.

Calvin will not let the verdict be quite so tidy. He concedes the philology, that the noun properly signifies a covering and the verb means to smear with pitch in its simple form and to expiate only in the intensive; and then doubts not that Moses alludes to a metaphorical meaning, since the law requires a covering to conceal our transgressions. His real argument is from the furniture rather than the grammar: it seems to him a tame explanation that Moses spoke literally of the cover, when he would have the cherubim turn their faces toward it and God promises to give his answers from it — by these honourable distinctions it is exalted above the ark. Clarke reaches the same sense by the metaphor itself: by an act of pardon sins are represented as covered, so that they no longer appear in the eye of divine justice to displease, irritate and call for punishment, and the offender is covered from the stroke of the broken law.

Gill, alone of them, keeps both senses without choosing. It was no more than a cover of the ark, which was open at the top, this being the lid and exactly answering to it, as the dimensions show; and because the root in one form signifies to propitiate, some render it the propitiatory, which is favoured by the apostle and the rather since God is represented sitting on it as showing himself propitious. The old Greek version, he notes, takes in both senses and renders it the propitiatory covering. Ellicott attends to the material and reckons the cost: not shittim wood overlaid with a plating of gold but a solid mass of the pure metal, calculated at seven hundred and fifty pounds Troy in weight and above twenty-five thousand pounds in value, the lavish outlay being intended to show that this was the object in which the accessories of worship culminated, the crowning glory of the material tabernacle.

The use follows from the name. Clarke records that on and before this the high priest was to sprinkle the blood of the expiatory sacrifices on the great day of atonement, and that it was here God promised to meet the people, since here was the symbol of the divine presence, between the cherubim at either end — whence it is so often said that he dwelleth between the cherubim. Wesley states the figure in a line, a type of Christ the great propitiation, whose satisfaction covers our transgressions and comes between us and the curse we deserve. Calvin argues it from the law's own pressure: as long as the law stands forth before God's face it subjects us to his wrath and curse, so that the blotting out of our guilt must be interposed before God can be reconciled with us.
18:
What a cherub was is the question, and nobody claims to have settled it. Clarke says outright that what these were we cannot distinctly say, reports the general supposition that a cherub was a creature with four heads and one body drawn from the noblest of their kinds — the lion among wild beasts, the bull among tame, the eagle among birds and man at the head of all, so that they might be representatives of all nature — and adds that the term often means a figure of any kind, such as was sculptured on stone, engraved on metal, carved on wood or embroidered on cloth. Ellicott sets out three schools: those who hold the proper figure to be a bull or ox and take these for winged bulls not unlike the Assyrian; those who regard them as still more composite, like the Egyptian sphinxes; and the predominant opinion, which he follows, that they were simply human figures with the addition of a pair of wings, bearing in that case a considerable resemblance to the figures so often seen inside Egyptian arks, sheltering an emblem of deity with their wings.

Gill lists the guesses too and then rejects a string of identifications rather than proposing a form: they were emblems not of the two Testaments, as many of the ancients held, nor of the angels, since they are distinguished from them, much less of the persons of the Godhead, but of the saints and true believers of both dispensations, signified by the number two and made of gold to denote their worth in the esteem of Christ. Calvin takes the opposite side of that same question and is content with less. He prefers the derivation that treats the word as meaning any image at all, refusing the reading that makes it mean like a boy, which he calls forced and refuted by the prophet who gives the name to the forms of a calf, a lion and an eagle as well as to the human form; and it is enough for him that the images were winged and represented angels, God having appointed angels, by whom he exercises his dominion, to be a symbol of his presence, so that the Prophets speak of him as dwelling between the cherubim as much as to say that he conversed familiarly with his people. Wesley agrees that they represent the holy angels, not by any effigy of an angel but by some emblem of the angelical nature.
20:
How they were made and how they stood is described more precisely than what they were. Ellicott glosses the beaten work as not cast but brought into shape by the hammer, and notes that in the Egyptian language the word for to hammer is the one from which, according to some, the name cherub comes; on the phrase about the two ends he gives the Hebrew as from the two ends, rising from either end of the mercy seat, and explains that they were not to be detached images made separately and then fastened on, but formed out of the same mass of gold and so part and parcel of it. Keil and Delitzsch say the same in their own words, that they were to be made out of the covering itself so as to form one whole with it and be inseparable from it. Gill notes that the situation is particularly explained lest it should be thought there were two at each end, whereas there was one at one end and another at the other, opposite each other and both pointing to the mercy seat.

The wings and the faces are read for what they signify. Keil and Delitzsch describe the posture exactly: the cherubs were to spread out their wings so as to form a screen over the covering, with their faces turned towards one another but inclining or stooping towards it. Ellicott observes that both wings of both figures were to be elevated and advanced so as to overshadow the mercy seat and, as it were, protect it, and marks the contrast with the Egyptian figures, in which one wing only has this position while the other is depressed and falls behind. Calvin refuses the obvious inference from the covering: that they covered the lid with their extended wings he does not imagine to have been done to hide it, but to mark the readiness of their obedience, the extension of the wings being equivalent to their being prepared to perform whatever God might command, and their faces turned towards the mercy seat because they are attentive to his will, and towards each other to indicate the harmony in which the angels are united.

Gill reads the outstretched wings as evidence about the shape: from them it appears they were in the form of winged creatures, like the seraphim of one prophet's vision and the living creatures of the others, and their wings did not hang down by them or at their sides but were stretched out upwards towards the heaven above their heads. Wesley gathers the whole posture into one sentence and then reads it: whatever the faces were, they looked one towards another and both downwards towards the ark, while their wings were stretched out so as to touch one another, which notes their attendance upon the Redeemer, their readiness to do his will, their presence in the assemblies of saints, and their desire to look into the mysteries of the gospel.
21:
Where the covering was to be placed is read by Gill for its doctrine rather than its carpentry. The mercy seat set above the ark, where the law was, signifies that there is no mercy but in a way of righteousness, or of satisfaction to the law of God and in consistence with the honour of it; and the cherubim over the mercy seat making a throne for the majesty of God in which he sat, with the ark below as a kind of footstool, shows that Christ stands between God and his law, mediator between God and men the transgressors of it, covering by fulfilling it the sins of his people which are violations of it, and being above it and having magnified it, able to suppress its charges and accusations. Keil and Delitzsch state the arrangement without the application, that the covering was to be put above upon the ark and the testimony put within.

The promise attached to the arrangement is what the rest of the witnesses fasten on. Keil and Delitzsch explain the posture of the cherubim by it: the reason the faces were to incline towards the covering is given in the next verse, since there, above the covering placed upon the ark containing the testimony, God would present himself to Moses — and they give the verb its precise force, to appoint, to present oneself to a person at an appointed place, to meet with him. Gill widens the appointment beyond Moses, to the high priest in later times when he should enter into the holy of holies, and to the people of God as represented by him when he should go in and inquire for them of the Lord.

What kind of meeting it was gets two answers that do not compete so much as divide the ground. Clarke keeps it to the place and the occasion: it was over the mercy seat, between the cherubim, that God chose to give the most especial manifestations of himself, where the divine glory was to be seen and where Moses was to come in order to consult him about the management of the people. Ellicott distinguishes two modes within the one promise, that God would meet his people there either literally, as when he answered inquiries of the high priest, or spiritually, as when he accepted incense and the blood of offerings and prayers offered to him through their appointed representatives, the priests; and he draws from the promise the name of the whole building, that it was for the purpose of thus meeting his people that the entire tabernacle was designed, whence its ordinary name was the Tent of Meeting, which our version renders less happily as the tabernacle of the congregation.

Clarke closes with an application he takes from an older commentator and traces to the rabbis, that the heart of man may be likened to God's sanctuary: as in the sanctuary the divine glory dwelt, because there were the ark, the tables and the cherubim, so in the heart of man it is meet that a place be made for the divine Majesty to dwell in, and that it be the holy of holies. This, he adds, is a doctrine most implicitly taught by the apostles, the necessity of having the heart made a habitation of God through the Spirit being strongly and frequently insisted on throughout the New Testament.
23:
Why a table belongs in the building is answered from the logic of a house. Gill puts it briefly: as the sanctuary was a house for God to dwell in, he would have the proper furniture of a house, a table and a candlestick and the rest; and he fixes its place, not in the holy of holies, where nothing but the ark stood, but in the holy place, on the north side. Clarke quotes an older divine to the same effect. The mystery of the tabernacle was that it should be a place for the habitation of Divinity to be fixed in, a type of God's future dwelling in Christ's human nature; and once a dwelling is granted, everything suitable to a house follows. Hence there must be a table and a candlestick, because that was the ordinary furniture of a room; the table must have its dishes and spoons and bowls and covers, though they were never used, and always be furnished with bread; the candlestick must have its lamps continually burning; a continual fire must be kept upon the altar as the focus of the house; and provision must be brought in, which was done in the sacrifices, the part consumed upon the altar being God's own portion, since the altar is elsewhere called God's table and the sacrifice upon it his meat.

Henry works the image from the other end: the tabernacle being God's house, in which he was pleased to dwell among them, he would show that he kept a good house, and in a royal palace it was fit there should be a royal table. The loaves were twelve, one for each tribe, in two rows of six; and as the ark signified God's being present with them, so the loaves signified their being presented to God. Wesley repeats the reading closely.

What the bread was for Henry gives under three heads. It was a thankful acknowledgement of God's goodness in giving them their daily bread, manna in the wilderness and afterwards the corn of the land, whereby they owned their dependence upon Providence not only for the corn in the field but for the bread in the house. It was a token of their communion with God, this bread on God's table being of the same corn as the bread on their own, so that God and Israel did as it were eat together, a pledge of friendship and fellowship. And it was a type of the spiritual provision made in the church by the gospel for all that are made priests to our God, since in our Father's house there is bread enough and to spare.

Calvin arrives at nearly the same place by way of an objection. He recalls an ancient bishop, deservedly praised, who sold the sacred vessels in a famine to relieve the poor and excused himself by saying that our God, who does not eat or drink, has no need of patens and chalices — a saying little in accordance with this very command that bread should be offered to him. Calvin answers by the difference of the dispensations: had the bishop stripped the sacred table under the Law he would have spoken unseasonably what under the Gospel he spoke piously and wisely, because at the coming of Christ the shadows of the Law ceased. God would have the loaves deposited among the golden dishes, not because he had need of meat and drink, but that he might prescribe the duty of temperance to his people by deigning to have his table among them; for when they ate of the same wheat of which the sacred loaves were made, they were reminded that their meat was to be taken as if they sat before God and were his guests, and that the food by which man's life is sustained is in a manner sacred to him.
24:
The plating and the edging are read for their purpose. Gill says the table was covered with a plate of gold so that the wood was not seen, and takes it to denote either the excellency of Christ's human nature, pure and spotless, or rather of his divine nature, which is said elsewhere to be as the most fine gold. Ellicott gives the practical reason and a classification with it: like the ark and the altar of incense, the table was to be overlaid with plates of gold, being a species of altar on which lay offerings to God and, standing close to the divine presence, requiring to be made of the best materials. On the crown he prefers a plainer word, a border or edging of gold, something to prevent what was placed on the table from readily falling off. Keil and Delitzsch describe the same fittings and add that the vessels to stand upon the table were to be of pure gold, the large deep plates being those in which the shewbread was not only brought to the table but placed upon it.

The band round the table is the one fitting nobody can place with confidence. Gill reports that the Jewish teachers are divided about it, some saying it was above, running round the table, and others that it was below, fixed from foot to foot at the four corners, with the board of the table laid upon it. Ellicott calls it a band or framing rather than a border, and settles the question from a monument rather than a text: the representation of the table of shewbread on the Arch of Titus at Rome gives the best idea of it, a flat bar about midway between the top of the table and its feet, connecting the four legs together and so keeping them in place, its golden edging being only for ornament.

The rings and poles repeat the arrangement made for the ark, and are read against it. Ellicott notes that the table, like the ark, would have to be carried from place to place, and that though it was less sacred than the ark provision was still made for carrying it; the four corners named are not the top corners but the bottom ones, so that the table, like the ark, was when carried to be elevated above the shoulders of the bearers — which again is how it is borne on the Arch of Titus. On the clause fixing where the rings went he admits defeat: the meaning is not very clear, for if the framing had been at the bottom of the legs we might have understood that the rings were attached opposite the places where it was inserted into them, but the framing appears to have been halfway up the legs while the rings were at the bottom, so that they could only have been opposite it in a loose and vague sense. Gill offers the old versions, which render the preposition as under rather than over against, and the rabbinic view that the rings were fixed to the feet over against the top of the band; and of the poles he says only that they were made in like manner as those for the ark, and of the same wood.
29:
The four vessels are named in a list and guessed at one by one, Gill saying of the first only that the shewbread loaves were set upon them. Clarke takes the dishes for the deep bowls in which they kneaded the mass out of which the shewbread was made; the spoons for censers, on which they put up the incense, as seems pretty evident from the places where the same word is used and the instrument is always represented as filled with incense; the covers for a large cup or tankard in which pure wine was kept on the table along with the bread for libations, poured out before the Lord every sabbath when the old bread was removed and the new laid on; and the bowls, from a root meaning to clear away, remove or empty, for either the sieves by which the Levites cleansed the wheat — since it is asserted that the grain was sowed, reaped, ground, sifted, kneaded and baked by the Levites themselves — or the ovens in which the bread was baked, or else vessels dipped into the tankard to draw out the wine.

Ellicott answers the same four from monuments rather than roots. The dishes were probably large bowls in which the loaves were brought to the table, such bowls being common in the Egyptian wall decorations; the so-called spoons were small pots in which the incense was put and burnt, two of which appear upon the table on the Arch of Titus; and the covers and bowls were flagons and chalices to contain the drink offerings which were necessary accompaniments of every meat offering. On the closing clause he prefers the reading in the margin, to pour out withal rather than to cover withal, since drink offerings were poured out in libation. Gill adds a rabbinic detail about the dishes, that they were of the form of the bread and of two sorts, one of gold and one of iron, the bread being baked in the iron one and put into the golden one until the morrow of the sabbath, when it was set in order upon the table, the two being distinguished as much by their use as by their metal.
30:
The name of the bread is explained two ways, and Clarke will not choose between them. It is literally bread of faces, he says, so called either because the loaves were placed before the presence or face of God in the sanctuary, or because they were made square, as the Jews will have it — probably cubes, each side presenting the same appearance, whence the loaves of faces; though the Hebrew text seems to him to intimate the first sense, since the Lord says they were set before my face. Ellicott gives simply bread of face or bread of presence. Gill describes the arrangement: twelve cakes set in two rows, standing a whole week and renewed every sabbath, the old ones eaten by the priests and new ones set in their place, so that they were always before the Lord. Clarke adds that on the top of each row there stood a golden dish with frankincense, burned before the Lord as a memorial at the end of the week when the loaves were changed, the priests taking the old ones for their domestic use.

On what the bread meant, one witness declines where two others venture. Gill makes it a memorial of the goodness of God in daily providing bread for Israel, presented as a thankful acknowledgment of it and being the same they ate at their own tables; and being eaten by the priests it was expressive of the communion between God and them, they being guests of his and feeding on the same provisions. Keil and Delitzsch are more careful about the direction of the gift: the loaves were to lie before the face of God as a meat-offering presented by the children of Israel, not as food for God but as a symbol of the spiritual food which Israel was to prepare, a figurative representation of the calling it had received from him, so that the bread and wine upon the table, as the fruit of the labour bestowed on the soil of its inheritance, were a symbol of its spiritual labour in the kingdom of God. Clarke refuses to add a conjecture of his own: it is more difficult, he says, to ascertain the use of these or what they represented than almost any other emblem in the whole Jewish economy, and many have conjectured their meaning without his feeling any disposition to increase their number.

Gill follows the loaves into their typology as well. The pure and unleavened cakes may denote the purity, simplicity and sincerity of the church and people of God, who are all one bread, being without the leaven of malice and wickedness; and the number twelve answers to the twelve tribes, that is to the whole spiritual Israel of God.
31:
The shape is described consistently, and only the names of the parts are disputed. Clarke sets it out as one shaft with six branches proceeding from it, adorned at equal distances with six flowers like lilies and as many bowls and knops placed alternately, a lamp on each branch and one on the top of the shaft, so that there were seven in all, lighted every evening and extinguished every morning. Henry adds that it was not hollow but solid, and divides its qualities: it was magnificent and a great ornament to the place, the branches having not only bowls for the oil and the kindled wick, for necessity, but knops and flowers for ornament; and it was convenient, contrived both to scatter the light and to keep the tabernacle clean of smoke and snuffs. Ellicott corrects the three terms to cups, pomegranates and blossoms, notes that the cups are afterwards said to be like almond blossoms, and insists that all of it was of one piece with the stem and branches and not separate ornaments put together. Keil and Delitzsch gloss each word: the base upon which the candelabrum stood, the reed or hollow stem rising from it, cups resembling the calix of a flower, knobs in a spherical shape, and flowers in the form of buds.

Clarke claims an unusual degree of certainty about this one object, and says why. We are not so certain of the precise form of any instrument or utensil of the tabernacle or temple, he writes, as we are of this, the golden table and the two silver trumpets; for after the overthrow of Jerusalem the conqueror had the golden candlestick, the golden table, the silver trumpets and the book of the law taken out of the temple and carried in triumph to Rome, where they were lodged in a temple consecrated to the goddess of Peace. At the foot of the hill stand the ruins of an arch on which that triumph is represented and the monuments of the procession sculptured, the candlestick and the table and the trumpets among them; and a correct model of it, taken on the spot, stood before him as he wrote. The candlestick there is less ornamented than in many prints and scarcely measures three feet, which makes him think the sculpture smaller than the original. Then the reflection he cannot keep out: to see these sacred articles, given up by the God who ordered them made after a pattern he had himself exhibited, gracing the triumph of a heathen emperor and at last consecrated to an idol, affords melancholy reflections to a pious mind — though he answers himself that they had accomplished the end for which they were instituted, the true light being by then come.

Why a candlestick was needed at all is turned by three witnesses into a statement about the age. Gill notes that it was another piece of household furniture, useful especially in a house with no windows, as the tabernacle had none; it stood in the holy place on the south side, opposite the table, and its use is to hold forth the light put into it, for it has none of itself. Henry and Wesley draw the same inference at more length: the tabernacle had no windows by which to let in the light of the day, and all its light was candle-light, which intimates the comparative darkness of that dispensation, while the Sun of righteousness had not as yet risen nor the day-star from on high visited his church. Yet God left not himself without witness, nor them without instruction, since the commandment was a lamp and the law a light, and the prophets were branches from that lamp giving light in their several ages; and the church is still dark, as the tabernacle was, compared with what it will be in heaven.
32:
How the thing was put together is described by Keil and Delitzsch more exactly than by anyone else, and they build it up from the base. From the sides of the upright stem in the middle there were to be six branches, three on either side; on each of these there were to be three cups in the form of an almond-flower with knob and flower, and on the central stem four such cups with their knobs and flowers. At the point where each of the three pairs of arms branched off from the main stem a knob was so placed that the arms should proceed from the knob, or from the stem immediately above it; and the knobs and pipes of the three pairs were to be combined with the candlestick so as to form one whole, all of one kind of beaten work, pure gold. Their summary is that upon the vase rose an upright central pipe from which three side pipes branched out one above another on either side and curved upwards in a quadrant to the level of the stem, with a calix and a knob and blossom four times on that stem, a knob wherever the side pipes branched off and the fourth higher up between the top branches and the end.

Two smaller questions are left open. Keil and Delitzsch report an explanation they reject, that of those who take the words for knob and flower as standing in apposition to the words before them, so that the flower-cups would consist of knobs with flowers bursting from them; apart from the singular idea of calling a bulb with a flower bursting from it a flower-cup, they answer, the opening verse decidedly precludes it, since there cups, knobs and flowers are named as three separate things. Ellicott raises the other: it is not quite clear whether the three cups on a branch were consecutive, or whether each cup held a pomegranate on which followed a lily blossom, and he judges that a well-known representation accords best with the latter view; he adds that the ornamentation was the same in every branch, but that in the longer branches the triple series was probably repeated oftener, and that by the candlestick in the verse about the four cups must be meant the central shaft, viewed as that whereto all the rest is accessory. Gill passes on a rabbinic detail of scale, that from the middle of the knop two branches were drawn out on either side, and that the height of the whole was eighteen hands' breadth.

Calvin reads the seven lights as a lesson about how God is to be worshipped. God would have seven bright lamps burning day and night in the tabernacle, that the people might know they were directed by God himself as to how they were to worship him aright, and that a light was set before their eyes which might disperse all the darkness of error; and lest they should obscure his worship with their gross inventions, but rather, intent on the instruction of the Law, seek after God with a pure and enlightened mind in all the ceremonies. He marks the distinction between the rule of true religion and the superstitions of the Gentiles, who were carried away by their blind devotions into circuitous and erring ways, so that nothing in them was straight; for unless we have divine teaching to enlighten us, our own reason will beget nothing but mere vanity. But it was not enough, he adds, that the right way should be pointed out, unless their eyes were opened to see it, since men are sometimes blind in the very midst of light — which happened to the Israelites themselves, who held fast the external form of the Law and were nevertheless degenerate, conceiving in obedience to their carnal reason that religion consisted in ceremonies.
37:
The lamps and the small instruments are identified without much dispute. Gill counts the seven, six on the tops of the branches and the seventh on the shaft that ran up the middle, and takes them for the gifts and graces of the Spirit or the ministers of the Gospel. Ellicott gives the Hebrew idiom, thou shalt make its lamps seven, notes that each branch as well as the stem was to have its own, and reports that the monument at Rome shows them as hemispherical bowls. On the instruments Ellicott is brief: pincers for trimming the wicks and removing loose portions, and dishes for receiving what was removed. Keil and Delitzsch name them snuffers and snuff-dishes and add that the second word elsewhere means an ash-pan, a vessel for carrying coal from the fire. Gill collects the rabbinic guesses: a sort of forks with which they took the wicks out of the oil, or else snuffers, though these are distinguished from tongs; and for the dishes, small cups holding the ashes of the lamp, or, on a view he thinks not improbable, vessels full of water into which the snuffings were dropped so that they might not smoke.

The talent of gold is the one place where the witnesses set about arithmetic, and they arrive at widely different sums. Keil and Delitzsch convert it to eight hundred and twenty-two thousand Parisian grains and remark that from this quantity a candlestick of very considerable size was possible, though the size is nowhere given; a conjecture they report would make it match the table, a cubit and a half in height and the same in breadth. Gill gives the common talent at sixty pounds and the sacred at double, and the value on one bishop's reckoning at over five thousand pounds. Clarke works the same bishop's figures from the half-shekels the people contributed, dividing the total by the number of talents to get three thousand shekels to the talent, and reaches six thousand seven hundred and fifty pounds. Ellicott reports the spread, that there are various estimates of the weight and value of the Hebrew gold talent but none places it much below four thousand pounds while some carry it as high as ten or eleven thousand; and he notes that the pronoun in the clause refers to the artificer who would construct it.

The chapter closes as it opened, on the pattern, and Gill reads the charge strictly: Moses is to see the work done exactly according to the model he had a view of, in which everything was particularly described and nothing left to the will, humour and fancy of men. Calvin insists the vision is not the point but its object: it is certain that no mere vision is here in question, but that the external ornaments of the sanctuary have their spiritual object, as is plain from the explanation given by the martyr and by the Apostle.

Clarke reads the closing verse as a command issued after the whole description was finished, and then makes it a rule for something else. It appears to him that the Apostle had this command in view when he charged his son in the faith to hold fast the form of sound words he had heard of him; for the tabernacle was a type of the Church of God, built on the foundation of the prophets and apostles with Jesus Christ as the chief cornerstone, so that the doctrines delivered by the prophets, by Christ and by his apostles are essential to that church. As God gave the plan by which the tabernacle must be constructed, Clarke argues, so he gives the doctrines by which the Christian Church is to be modelled, and subordinate builders are to hold fast that form of sound words and build according to the pattern which has come through the express revelation of God.
